summary: Uruguay has one of South America's most open entry policies: Mercosur and associate-member nationals arrive on a national ID card, and citizens of the EU, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada and a long list of other countries enter visa-free for 90 days, extendable by another 90.

passportValidity.text: Uruguay requires a passport valid for the duration of your stay rather than a fixed six-month buffer, but airlines and onward countries often apply the stricter rule — six months is the safe margin. Mercosur and associate-member nationals may enter on a valid national identity card instead.

source.name: Uruguay — Dirección Nacional de Migración (Ministerio del Interior)
Uruguay — Dirección Nacional de Migración (Ministerio del Interior)

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: Uruguay has no yellow fever risk and does not require a certificate for entry. Vaccination matters only if your trip continues to Brazil, Paraguay or Bolivia, where risk areas and onward requirements do apply.

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not an entry requirement. Uruguayan private clinics are good but charge visitors directly, and treatment can be expensive by regional standards, so cover is recommended.

onwardTicket.text: Not systematically checked, though airlines and immigration officers may ask visa-free visitors for a return or onward ticket within the 90-day allowance and for an address in Uruguay.

source.name: Uruguay — Dirección Nacional de Migración (Ministerio del Interior)

proofOfFunds.text: No published amount and rarely asked of tourists; visa applicants must show bank statements covering the trip.

currencyLimits.text: Cash or negotiable instruments worth USD 10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared to customs on entry and exit. The rule is applied on the Buquebus ferries from Buenos Aires as well as at airports.

notes: Personal goods brought in by air are duty-free up to a published allowance — currently a few hundred US dollars, with a smaller allowance at land borders.
Fresh meat, dairy, fruit and plant material may not be brought in; agricultural controls are strict because of Uruguay's beef exports.
Cannabis is legal for residents but tourists may not buy it in pharmacies, and taking any amount across the border is a criminal offense in Argentina and Brazil.

payments.text: Uruguay is close to cashless: cards and contactless work almost everywhere, including buses in Montevideo and small cafés. Foreign cards attract an automatic VAT refund on restaurant and hotel bills, so paying by card is actively worth it. Keep a little cash for markets and rural roadside stalls.

safety.text: Uruguay is among the safest countries in South America and the tourist areas — Ciudad Vieja by day, Pocitos, Colonia, Punta del Este — are calm. Petty theft and occasional armed robbery do occur in parts of Montevideo, so avoid quiet streets in Ciudad Vieja after dark and the outer barrios, and do not leave anything visible in a parked car.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Uruguay Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to March is the southern-hemisphere summer, when the Atlantic beaches from Punta del Este to Cabo Polonio come alive; January is peak season and expensive, while March and November are warm and much quieter.

idp.text: Uruguay is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

driving.text: Uruguay is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Uruguay yet.

tips.text: Pay restaurant and hotel bills with a foreign-issued card: non-residents get the 22% VAT deducted automatically on tourism services, which is an instant discount rather than a form to fill in at the airport.

From late December to mid-February, Punta del Este and the coastal resorts fill with Argentine and Brazilian holidaymakers and prices can triple. Book months ahead for January, or travel in March or November instead.

The fastest route in is often the ferry from Buenos Aires to Colonia del Sacramento or Montevideo. Argentine and Uruguayan immigration are done side by side in the same hall before boarding, so you get both stamps in one line.
Cannabis is legal in Uruguay but only for registered residents — tourists cannot buy it in pharmacies, and carrying any across the border into Argentina or Brazil is a serious criminal offense.
Tap water is safe to drink throughout the country, and Uruguayans carry a thermos and a mate gourd everywhere — cafés and gas stations will refill your flask with hot water, usually free.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Uruguay?
faq.answer: Probably not. Uruguay waives visas for a very broad list of nationalities — the EU and EEA, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Israel, Russia and most of Latin America and the Caribbean — for tourist stays of up to 90 days. Mercosur and associate-member nationals can enter on a national ID card. Everyone else applies for a visa at a Uruguayan consulate.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Uruguay without a visa?
faq.answer: Ninety days per entry for most visa-free nationalities. The Dirección Nacional de Migración can grant one extension (prórroga) of a further 90 days if you apply before the first period runs out, giving up to 180 days in total.

faq.question: Can I enter Uruguay with a national ID card instead of a passport?
faq.answer: Yes, if you are a national of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador or Peru. Mercosur and associate-member citizens cross with a valid national identity document — the usual choice for the ferry from Buenos Aires — and stay 90 days. Bring a passport if you are connecting on from outside the bloc.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Uruguay?
faq.answer: No. United States passport holders enter visa-free for tourism for up to 90 days, with one 90-day extension available from Uruguayan immigration. There is no reciprocity fee and no advance authorization to buy.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Uruguay?
faq.answer: Yes. Apply to the Dirección Nacional de Migración in Montevideo or a regional office before your current 90 days expire. One extension of up to 90 days is normally granted for a small fee; you will need your passport, accommodation details and, sometimes, an onward ticket.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever certificate for Uruguay?
faq.answer: No. Uruguay has no yellow fever risk and does not ask arriving travelers for a certificate. It becomes relevant only if your trip continues to Brazil, Paraguay or Bolivia, which have their own risk areas and requirements.
